name: Don't Go Missing Public Wilderness Missing-Person Risk Zones
notice: Counts reflect compiled public-record reports of people who went missing in or near U.S. National Parks, National Forests and other wilderness areas, gathered for safety awareness. They are not official, complete or live National Park Service, Forest Service or search-and-rescue dispatch totals, and a higher count does not mean an area is unsafe to visit. Coordinates are approximate area centres, not last-seen points.
source: Derived from an open, public-record compilation of missing-person cases in and near national parks and wilderness areas (Kaggle: "Open Missing People Cases Inside National Parks"), cleaned by Don't Go Missing: names standardised, records for the same area merged, clearly mis-located records corrected or removed.

terrainBriefs.mountain: Ridges and deep drainages block cell signal, so service often disappears within minutes of the trailhead. Weather can turn quickly at elevation, steep or boulder-strewn terrain slows travel, and hikers who start late often turn around too late to beat dark.
terrainBriefs.forest: Dense timber, look-alike ridges and a web of unmarked roads and game trails make it easy to drift off route. Cell signal is patchy to absent away from main roads, and short days or rain can turn a day hike into a cold night out.
terrainBriefs.desert: Heat, scarce water and long sight lines that hide how far things really are are the main hazards. Washes and boulder fields look the same from every direction, signal is unreliable, and a short walk from a vehicle can become dangerous within hours.
terrainBriefs.canyon: Canyon walls block signal and GPS can wander, and the return trip is usually the hardest part. Heat, flash floods and loose rock leave little margin for a late turnaround.
terrainBriefs.wetland: Flat, featureless terrain with few landmarks, dense vegetation, heat and humidity make navigation hard. Trails can flood, and signal is patchy once you leave the roads.
terrainBriefs.coastal: Fog, tides, cliffs and cold water are the main hazards, and steep coastal terrain blocks signal more often than people expect. Routes that are safe at low tide can cut you off later in the day.
terrainBriefs.tropical: Steep, slippery volcanic terrain, sudden heavy rain, flash flooding in valleys and dense vegetation make it easy to get stuck or lost. Coverage drops fast away from roads and resorts.

zones.name: Yosemite National Park
zones.brief: Cell coverage is concentrated in Yosemite Valley and developed areas; most of the high country beyond the trailheads has none. Granite slabs and domes are slick when wet, spring snowmelt turns creek crossings and waterfalls deadly, and afternoon thunderstorms build fast above 8,000 ft. Many visitors underestimate distances and elevation, then turn around late.

zones.name: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
zones.brief: Dense forest, frequent fog and steep, look-alike ridges make it easy to drift off trail in the Smokies, and most of the park has no cell service. Weather swings sharply with elevation, and rain can raise creeks quickly.

zones.name: Grand Canyon National Park
zones.brief: Every Grand Canyon hike starts downhill, so the hard half comes last, often in extreme heat. Inner-canyon temperatures can run 20°F hotter than the rim, cell service drops away below the rim, and a wrong turn on an unmaintained route can strand a hiker far from water.

zones.name: Angeles National Forest
zones.brief: Steep, crumbly canyon terrain sits within sight of Los Angeles, which makes it feel safer than it is. Ridgelines block signal in the canyons, winter ice on peaks like Mount Baldy causes serious falls, and summer heat dehydrates hikers fast.

zones.name: Death Valley National Park
zones.brief: Extreme heat, long distances between water, and roads that look passable but are not define Death Valley. Most of the park has no cell service, and a vehicle breakdown or a short walk from a car can become a survival situation within hours in summer.

zones.name: Olympic National Park
zones.brief: Olympic National Park mixes temperate rainforest, glaciated peaks and wild coastline. Heavy rain, dense undergrowth and tide-dependent beach routes catch visitors out, and coverage is minimal once you leave the highway corridor.

zones.name: Plumas National Forest
zones.brief: Plumas National Forest is a maze of forest roads, timber and granite in the northern Sierra and southern Cascades. Coverage is patchy to absent away from towns, and snow can close roads and bury trails well into spring.

zones.name: Yellowstone National Park
zones.brief: Yellowstone combines huge distances, thermal ground that can be deadly off boardwalks, wildlife, and weather that can bring snow in any month. Cell service is limited to developed areas, and the backcountry is vast and sparsely travelled.

zones.name: Joshua Tree National Park
zones.brief: Joshua Tree looks open, but boulder fields and washes look alike from every direction, and summer heat is dangerous. Many hikers lose their bearings a short distance from the trail, and cell service is unreliable across much of the park.

zones.name: Mount Hood
zones.brief: Mount Hood weather changes fast and whiteouts are common above timberline. Climbers and hikers descending in poor visibility can drift into the wrong drainage, and coverage is unreliable on the upper mountain and in its canyons.

zones.name: Ocala National Forest
zones.brief: Ocala National Forest is flat, sandy scrub and dense pine where landmarks are scarce and trails cross many unmarked sand roads. Heat, humidity and afternoon storms add up quickly, and signal is patchy.
